I'm 22, 5'9", male, and started gymming almost three years ago, but really only took it a bit more seriously in the last year or so. Growing up, I've never really been into sports or any form of exercise so I've always been skinny, especially after the growth spurt. (My family always cooked meals at home, and early on I've developed a distaste for fast food and other junk food.) My family and friends have always commented on how skinny I was, and it stung a bit each time. I wanted to exercise but lacked interest in any team or contact sports and hated the "bro" culture that surrounded these sports (at least in my school).

Yet I didn't want to join a gym because they were expensive and, more importantly, my family would have thought that it was a very vain and almost narcissistic thing to do. So I exercised in secret. When I was home alone, I would use anything I could find to serve as a makeshift gym. To name a few: a clunky lawnmower battery served as a single dumbbell; a metal pole that was half of a beach umbrella stuck between two I-beams of the unfinished basement was a pull-up bar; a broken set of washer and dryer placed about two feet apart was used as a dip station, but could also be used for rack chins with that same metal pole if pieces of corrugated cardboard were added to prevent the pole from slipping. None of it was really safe or efficient (and I highly discourage anyone from doing it), but if anything, it got me into the mindset of exercising, even though I'm not sure if it made much physical difference.

The beginning of my sophomore year at university was when I decided to check out the gym, since membership was included in the tuition. At this point, I must have been 130 lbs, and I was more or less going in blind, with no routine or goals or even the knowledge of how to use most of the machines. But I went in, sticking to what little I knew and watching others to learn how to use the machines and eventually to learn different movements with both dumbbells and barbells. It was a long and arduous process, and I don't think I achieved much progress for the first few months, but in retrospect, I was again just getting into the routine of just exercising. I didn't take any supplements at all, and now I know that the seemingly lack of progress was due to not eating enough.

Still, I kept this exercising a secret, which was easy to do since my body didn't change much. It might have been because I was just used the secrecy, but I was also afraid that people would start judging me. I didn't want to admit to my own insecurities, and I didn't want others to think that my time working out was time wasted because I had nothing to show for it. And again, I didn't want people to think that I have become too concerned with my looks because that was the stereotype I had ingrained in my mind. But at this point, it was part of my routine to go, and I figured that if anyone asked why I went, I would just say, "I might as well--I'm already paying for it" or "It's an investment for my own health," both of which were true.

After two years, I must have gained only 10-15 lbs, hindered by the long winter and summer breaks away from the university, as well as lack of both supplements and tracking what I ate. Yes, nearly two years without any supplements (including protein shakes) because I didn't quite have the money for them and anyone who found them in my room would know that I worked out. Due to a conflict of class scheduling, I decided to take two months of classes during the summer between my junior and senior year, which also meant two months of gym time that I otherwise would have spent just sitting at home. And since I finally no longer shared a room starting that summer, I bought my first tub of whey. I think I started following a workout routine that I found online, although I can remember which one. The slightly shorter version of the story is that in the first week of classes of the Fall semester, the general reaction of my friends, having not seen them in three months, was "You've gotten huge! Have you been working out?" I think I only gained about 5 lbs that summer, but maybe my body fat percentage decreased or something. So clearly, working out was no longer a secret, but it felt nice to let the cat out of the bag in that way.

Now, I'm about 160 lbs, and of course still exercising because I genuinely enjoy it. People still occasionally ask if I work out and I'm always tempted to quote Captain Hammer, but I don't think most people would understand it and then I'd surely be a complete egotist to them. But I still always feel a bit of embarrassment when they ask and just sheepishly confirm that I do. It's been a long journey and it's far from over, but I'm starting to feel more pleased with how I look. The comments about being skinny have disappeared, although I still feel like I am sometimes. My family has commented on me getting bigger, but I'm not sure what they really think of it. But I've also stopped caring about what they would think of it.

tl;dr: I'm always trying to make me into a better version of myself, and it was foolish that I didn't do it sooner because I was afraid of what others would think even though I feel better and more comfortable in my own skin. Love yourself. If you don't, then work on something to change it and don't ever let the opinions of others stop you.
